Banning cuts off access via a servlet filter that runs on every authenticated request, not via revoking the token itself. The mechanism lives in **BannedUserAuthorizationFilter.java** (subsystem 9, Auth journeys & BDD harness), which per its flow edges CONSTRAINS/INJECTS **UserCacheService.java** (subsystem 6, Two-factor auth & user cache â€” 53 ext in-edges, the Firestore/Redis-backed cache holding the authoritative user record) and IMPORTS **BaseExceptionHandler.java** (subsystem 7) to reject the request. So the filter looks up the current user's cached status via UserCacheService, and if that status indicates banned, it short-circuits the request chain and returns an error (a 403-with-valid-token style rejection, the pattern subsystem 9's navigator explicitly calls out) rather than letting it reach the controller.

The status vocabulary itself â€” the enum value that marks an account as banned â€” is **AccountStatus.java** (subsystem 16, Status enums & OpenAPI contract, 52 ext in-edges), a pure supplier layer with no orchestration logic of its own; it's imported by AuthService.java, InMemoryUserCache.java/RedisUserCache.java, RegistrationService.java and others that read/write that status. So the causal chain is: an admin action sets AccountStatus on the user record â†’ UserCacheService serves that cached status â†’ BannedUserAuthorizationFilter checks it on every request and blocks access.

To see the exact status value and rejection response, open BannedUserAuthorizationFilter.java first, then UserCacheService.java.
